einzeiler: Gadi Eisenkot is trying to form an Israeli government, but every coalition path is…
kurzfassung: Following Israel's election without a clear winner, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has weeks to assemble a governing coalition. He faces immense hurdles, including whether to compromise with ultra-Orthodox parties or seek partnerships with Arab lawmakers. Every potential alliance risks alienating voters, threatening both his political survival and Benjamin Netanyahu's potential return to power.
stichpunkte: Gadi Eisenkot has a strict timeline of four to six weeks to form a governing coalition after an inconclusive election.
Benjamin Netanyahu serves as the caretaker prime minister, benefiting politically if negotiations stall and new elections are called.
Forming an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties conflicts with Eisenkot's campaign promises regarding military service and secular education.
Negotiating with ultra-Orthodox parties carries the risk that their leaders might ultimately defect back to Netanyahu.
Arab citizens make up 20 percent of Israel's population, and their parties secured a record 19 seats in the recent election.
Mansour Abbas and the Islamist party Ra'am have expressed a strong desire to participate in government, unlike historical boycotts by Arab politicians.
Eisenkot's mandatory coalition principles, such as recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization, create a painful loyalty-oath dynamic for Arab voters.
Key coalition partners like Avigdor Lieberman adamantly refuse to sit in a government with Arab parties.
Excluding Arab parties entirely raises critical questions about democratic representation and Israel's long-standing claims about minority rights.
Alternative options like a minority government remain highly unstable, leaving Eisenkot with a set of deeply radioactive choices.

clips.text: If the opposition leader fails to build a government, the opportunity passes to Netanyahu, potentially leading to dissolved parliament and new elections where the incumbent holds a major advantage.

clips.hook: Why the ultra-Orthodox pose a coalition dilemma
clips.text: Ultra-Orthodox parties demand total draft exemptions for young men studying in religious schools alongside generous government subsidies, directly contradicting the opposition's platform.

clips.hook: The vital role of Arab citizens in Israeli society
clips.text: Arab citizens constitute a fifth of the population, holding full citizenship and working extensively across the middle class, including healthcare positions that serve Israeli patients and soldiers.

clips.hook: How the right wing visualizes an opposition government
clips.text: An artificial intelligence campaign video depicted a future administration with Arab lawmakers vetoing security crackdowns while showing enthusiasm exclusively for Palestinian statehood discussions.

clips.hook: The ultimate test of Israel's democratic claims
clips.text: When critics previously accused the nation of repression, officials pointed to minority voting rights and parliamentary access as proof, raising questions when those very representatives are excluded from power.

beschreibung:
More than two weeks after one of the most consequential elections in Israel’s history, there is still uncertainty about who will lead the country.
The spotlight has fallen on the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to make all kinds of deals to build a coalition that could run the government.
David Halbfinger, The New York Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, explains the compromises that Mr. Eisenkot will need to make, and what will happen if he can’t.
Guest: David M. Halbfinger, the Jerusalem bureau chief for The New York Times.
